chapter_name: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines

chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: triangles from three lengths first, then triangles from angles, then altitudes and kinds of triangles. Every rule is reached by building a triangle and asking when it cannot be built, so a rule such as the triangle inequality is a finding and not a fact to memorise.

points.title: Try first, name later
points.text: The hook video leaves one question open: what happens when three corner points lie on a straight line. The compass construction and the triangle inequality arrive only after the student has tried to build triangles.

points.title: When a triangle cannot be built
points.text: For lengths, for two sides and an angle, and for two angles and a side, the chapter asks when the construction fails. Each failure leads to a rule: the triangle inequality, an angle below 180 degrees, and two angles that add to less than 180 degrees.

points.title: Parallel lines explain the angles
points.text: One line drawn through a vertex parallel to the opposite side explains why two angles must add to less than 180 degrees, how to find the third angle, and why the three angles always add to 180 degrees.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic with one video per concept and a practice concept at the end; interactive tools appear only where handling the figure is the idea. The book's questions follow in their own topic, one question and one video per concept.

concepts.concept_name: A frame of three beams

content.text:
A triangle is the most basic closed shape. As we know, it consists of:
three corner points, that we call the vertex of the triangle, and
three line segments or the sides of the triangle that join the pairs of vertices.
Triangles come in various shapes.
Observe the symbol used to denote a triangle and how the triangles are named using their vertices. While naming a triangle, the vertices can come in any order.
The three sides meeting at the corners give rise to three angles that we call the angles of the triangle. For example, in ∆ABC, these angles are ∠CAB, ∠ABC, ∠BCA, which we simply denote as ∠A, ∠B and ∠C, respectively.

content.text:
1. Picture three wooden beams of a shed roof, nailed together at their ends to make a triangle frame. The three nails are the corners, called vertices, and the beams are the sides.
2. Make a guess before the next step: if the top nail is pressed down until all three nails lie on one straight line, do we still have a triangle?
3. A triangle can be named with its vertices in any order: ∆ABC, ∆BCA and ∆CAB are the same triangle. Its angles are ∠A, ∠B and ∠C.

concepts.concept_name: Building with a ruler alone

content.text:
7.1 Equilateral Triangles
Among all the triangles, the equilateral triangles are the most symmetric ones. These are triangles in which all the sides are of equal lengths. Let us try constructing them.
Construct a triangle in which all the sides are of length 4 cm.
How did you construct this triangle and what tools did you use? Can this construction be done only using a marked ruler (and a pencil)?
Constructing this triangle using just a ruler is certainly possible. But this might require several trials. Say we draw the base, let us call it AB, of length 4 cm, and mark the third point C using a ruler such that AC = 4 cm. This may not lead to BC also having a length of 4 cm. If this happens, we will have to keep making attempts to mark C till we get BC to be 4 cm long.
How do we make this construction more efficient?

content.text:
1. Predict first: if AB = 4 cm and C is marked 4 cm from A, will BC also be 4 cm?
2. An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal, so each side is 4 cm here.
3. With a ruler alone, C is moved and measured again and again until both AC and BC are 4 cm: it works, but it takes several trials.

concepts.concept_name: Two arcs find the third corner

content.text:
Recall solving a similar problem in the previous year using a compass (in the Chapter 'Playing with Constructions'). We had to mark the top point of a 'house' which is 5 cm from two other points. The method we used to get that point can also be used here.
After constructing AB = 4 cm, we can do the following.
Step 1: Using a compass, construct a sufficiently long arc of radius 4 cm from A. The point C is somewhere on this arc. How do we mark it?
Step 2: Construct another arc of radius 4 cm from B. Let C be the point of intersection of the arcs.
The construction ensures that both AC and BC are of length 4 cm. Can you see why?
Step 3: Join AC and BC to get the required equilateral triangle.

content.text:
1. Predict first: every point on an arc of radius 4 cm from A is how far from A?
2. The arc from A holds all the places that are 4 cm from A, and the arc from B holds all the places that are 4 cm from B. The point where they cross is on both, so it is 4 cm from each end.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a triangle in which all the sides are of length 4 cm, and explain why AC and BC are both 4 cm.
1. Draw the base AB of length 4 cm.
2. Step 1: with the compass set to 4 cm and the point on A, draw a long arc above the base.
3. Step 2: keep the compass at 4 cm, put the point on B, and draw a second arc that crosses the first.
4. Mark the crossing point C. It is on the arc from A, so AC = 4 cm, and on the arc from B, so BC = 4 cm.
5. Step 3: join AC and BC. All three sides are 4 cm.
Answer: An equilateral triangle ABC with AB = BC = CA = 4 cm

concepts.concept_name: Constructing a triangle of sides 4, 5 and 6

content.text:
7.2 Constructing a Triangle When its Sides are Given
How do we construct triangles that are not equilateral?
Construct a triangle of sidelength 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm.
As in the previous case, this triangle can also be constructed using just a marked ruler. But it will involve several trials.
How do we construct this triangle more efficiently?
Choose one of the given lengths to be the base of the triangle: say 4 cm. Draw the base. Let A and B be the base vertices, and call the third vertex C. Let AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm.
Like we did in the case of equilateral triangles, let us first get all the points that are at a 5 cm distance from A. These points lie on the circle whose centre is A and has radius 5 cm. The point C must lie somewhere on this circle. How do we find it?
We will make use of the fact that the point C is 6 cm away from B. Construct an arc of radius 6 cm from B.
Let us summarise the steps of construction, noting that constructing full circles is not necessary to get the third vertex.
Step 1: Construct the base AB with one of the side lengths. Let us choose AB = 4 cm.
Step 2: From A, construct a sufficiently long arc of radius 5 cm.
Step 3: From B, construct an arc of radius 6 cm such that it intersects the first arc.
Step 4: The point where both the arcs meet is the required third vertex C. Join AC and BC to get ∆ABC.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if C is 5 cm from A and 6 cm from B, how many arcs do we need to find it?
2. The circle of radius 5 cm around A holds every point 5 cm from A; C must be one of them.
3. The arc of radius 6 cm around B holds every point 6 cm from B; the crossing point is the only place that is 5 cm from A and 6 cm from B.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm.
1. Step 1: draw the base AB = 4 cm.
2. Step 2: with the compass set to 5 cm and the point on A, draw a long arc above the base.
3. Step 3: set the compass to 6 cm, put the point on B and draw an arc that crosses the first arc.
4. Step 4: the crossing point is C. It is 5 cm from A and 6 cm from B. Join AC and BC.
5. Check with the ruler: AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm.
Answer: Triangle ABC with AB = 4 cm, AC = 5 cm and BC = 6 cm

concepts.concept_name: Why the crossing point is the third vertex, and isosceles triangles

content.text:
The required point C is one of the points of intersection of the two circles.
The reason why the point of intersection is the third vertex is the same as for equilateral triangles. This point lies on both the circles. Hence its distance from A is the radius of the circle centred at A (5 cm) and its distance from B is the same as the radius of the circle centred at B (6 cm).
We have seen that triangles having all three equal sides are called equilateral triangles. Those having two equal sides are called isosceles triangles.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the two full circles cross in two points. Does either one give a triangle?
2. Both crossing points are on both circles, so both give a triangle with the same three sides, one above the base and one below.
3. A triangle with all three sides equal is equilateral. A triangle with two equal sides is isosceles. An equilateral triangle also has two equal sides.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a triangle with sidelengths 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm and say what kind of triangle it is.
1. Take the side of 6 cm as the base AB.
2. From A draw an arc of radius 4 cm, and from B draw an arc of radius 4 cm. They cross at C.
3. C is 4 cm from A and 4 cm from B, so AC = BC = 4 cm.
4. Two sides are equal, so the triangle is isosceles.
Answer: An isosceles triangle with sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm

concepts.concept_name: Practice: build triangles from three sides

content.text:
Choose a base, draw an arc of one length from each end, and join the crossing point to both ends.
Equal radii give two equal sides.
Three equal sides make an equilateral triangle, two equal sides make an isosceles triangle.

concepts.concept_name: Construct (triangles from three sides)

content.text:
Construct (triangles from three sides): Construct triangles having the following sidelengths (all the units are in cm): (a) 4, 4, 6 (b) 3, 4, 5 (c) 1, 5, 5 (d) 4, 6, 8 (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5. Say what kind of triangle each is.
1. Each set satisfies the check: the two shorter lengths add to more than the longest (4 + 4 > 6, 3 + 4 > 5, 1 + 5 > 5, 4 + 6 > 8, 3.5 + 3.5 > 3.5), so each triangle can be built.
2. For each set draw the longest side as the base, then an arc of one of the other lengths from each end.
3. (a) 4, 4, 6 has two equal sides: isosceles. (b) 3, 4, 5 has three different sides: scalene. (c) 1, 5, 5 has two equal sides: isosceles, with a very short base.
4. (d) 4, 6, 8 has three different sides: scalene. (e) 3.5, 3.5, 3.5 has three equal sides: equilateral.
Answer: All five can be built: (a) isosceles, (b) scalene, (c) isosceles, (d) scalene, (e) equilateral

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (equilateral and isosceles triangles), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (equilateral and isosceles triangles), Q1: A circle is drawn with its centre marked, and some points are marked on the circle. Use the points on the circle and/or the centre to form isosceles triangles.
1. Mark the centre O and two points P and Q on the circle. Join OP, OQ and PQ.
2. OP and OQ are both radii of the same circle, so OP = OQ and triangle OPQ is isosceles.
3. Choosing P and Q so that PQ is also equal to the radius makes all three sides equal: an equilateral triangle.
4. Three points on the circle can also give an isosceles triangle: take P and Q, then take R halfway between them on the circle, so that RP = RQ.
Answer: Any two points on the circle with the centre give an isosceles triangle; two points whose distance is one radius give an equilateral triangle

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (equilateral and isosceles triangles), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (equilateral and isosceles triangles), Q2: Two circles of the same size have centres A and B, and each circle passes through the centre of the other. Then three circles of the same size have centres A, B and C, and each circle passes through the centres of the other two. Use the points on the circles and/or their centres to form isosceles and equilateral triangles.
1. Two circles: each passes through the other's centre, so the radius equals AB. Let C and D be the two points where the circles cross.
2. C is on the circle at A, so AC = AB, and on the circle at B, so BC = AB. All three sides of triangle ABC are equal: it is equilateral. In the same way triangle ABD is equilateral.
3. AC = AD because both are radii of the circle at A, so triangle ACD is isosceles; triangle BCD is isosceles in the same way.
4. Three circles: A, B and C are the centres and every pair of centres is one radius apart, so triangle ABC is equilateral. Each pair of circles crosses in two points, and each crossing point together with those two centres gives another equilateral triangle.
5. Any point on a circle with the centre and another point on the same circle gives an isosceles triangle, as in the single circle.
Answer: Triangles ABC and ABD are equilateral, and ACD and BCD are isosceles; with three circles ABC is equilateral and each crossing point forms more equilateral triangles

concepts.concept_name: Lengths that fail: 3, 4, 8 and 2, 3, 6

content.text:
Are Triangles Possible for any Lengths?
Can one construct triangles having any given sidelengths? Are there lengths for which it is impossible to construct a triangle? Let us explore this.
Construct a triangle with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm, and 8 cm.
What is happening? Are you able to construct the triangle?
Here is another set of lengths: 2 cm, 3 cm, and 6 cm. Check if a triangle is possible for these sidelengths.
Try to find more sets of lengths for which a triangle construction is impossible. See if you can find any pattern in them.
We see that a triangle is possible for some sets of lengths and not possible for others. How do we check if a triangle exists for a given set of lengths? One way is to actually try to construct the triangle and check if it is possible. Is there a more efficient way to check this?

content.text:
1. Predict first: with a base of 8 cm, can an arc of 3 cm from one end ever meet an arc of 4 cm from the other end?
2. The two arcs reach only 3 cm and 4 cm from the two ends of an 8 cm base, which is 7 cm in all. They fall short and never cross, so there is no third vertex.
3. The same happens for 2, 3 and 6: 2 + 3 = 5 is less than 6.
4. Look for the pattern in other failing sets, such as 1, 2, 5 or 4, 5, 10: the two shorter lengths together are less than the longest.

content.text:
Worked example: Try to construct a triangle with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm, then 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm, and say what happens to the arcs.
1. Take 8 cm as the base AB. Draw an arc of 3 cm from A and an arc of 4 cm from B.
2. The arc from A reaches 3 cm along the base and the arc from B reaches 4 cm back, which covers 3 + 4 = 7 cm of the 8 cm. They do not meet.
3. For 2, 3 and 6, take 6 cm as the base. The arcs of 2 cm and 3 cm cover 2 + 3 = 5 cm of the 6 cm and do not meet.
4. In both sets the two shorter lengths add to less than the longest: 3 + 4 = 7 < 8 and 2 + 3 = 5 < 6.
Answer: No triangle can be built for 3, 4, 8 or for 2, 3, 6: the arcs never meet

concepts.concept_name: A direct path and a roundabout path

content.text:
Triangle Inequality
Consider the lengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm. Does there exist a triangle having these as sidelengths?
To tackle this question, let us study a property of triangles. Imagine a small plot of plain land having a tent, a tree, and a pole. Imagine you are at the entrance of the tent and want to go to the tree. Which is the shorter path: (i) the straight-line path to the tree (the red path) or (ii) the straight-line path from the tent to the pole, followed by the straight-line path from the pole to the tree (the yellow path)?
Clearly, the direct straight-line path from the tent to the tree is shorter than the roundabout path via the pole. In fact, the direct straight-line path is the shortest possible path to the tree from the tent.
Will the direct path between any two points be shorter than the roundabout path via a third point? Clearly, the answer is yes.

content.text:
1. Predict first: on a plot, which is shorter, going straight from the tent to the tree or going from the tent to the pole and then to the tree?
2. The straight path is the shortest possible path between two points. Going through a third point adds a bend, so the walk is longer, unless the pole lies on the straight path itself.
3. Three points that are not on one line form a triangle. This gives the idea of the next concept: each side is a direct path, and the other two sides together are the roundabout path.

content.text:
Worked example: A tent, a tree and a pole are the three corners of a plot. The tent to the tree is 30 m in a straight line, the tent to the pole is 20 m and the pole to the tree is 25 m. Which way is shorter?
1. Direct path from the tent to the tree: 30 m.
2. Roundabout path from the tent to the pole and then to the tree: 20 m + 25 m = 45 m.
3. 30 m is less than 45 m, so the direct path is shorter.
4. The same holds for every pair of the three corners: each direct path is shorter than the roundabout path through the third corner.
Answer: The direct path of 30 m is shorter than the roundabout path of 45 m

concepts.concept_name: The triangle inequality: 10, 15, 30 and 3, 3, 7

content.text:
Can this understanding be used to tell something about the existence of a triangle having sidelengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm?
Let us suppose that there is a triangle for this set of lengths. Remember that at this point we are not sure about the existence of the triangle but we are only supposing that it exists. Let us draw a rough diagram.
If this triangle were possible, then the direct path between any two vertices should be shorter than the roundabout path via the third vertex. Is this true for our rough diagram?
Let us consider the paths between B and C. Direct path length = BC = 10 cm. Roundabout path length = BA + AC = 15 cm + 30 cm = 45 cm. Is the direct path length shorter than the roundabout path length? Yes.
Let us now consider the paths between A and B. Direct path length = AB = 15 cm. Roundabout path length = AC + CB = 30 cm + 10 cm = 40 cm. Is the direct path length shorter than the roundabout path length? Yes.
Finally, consider paths between C and A. Direct path length = CA = 30 cm. Roundabout path length = CB + BA = 10 cm + 15 cm = 25 cm. Is the direct path length shorter than the roundabout path length? In this case, the direct path is longer, which is absurd. Can such a triangle exist? No.
Therefore, a triangle having sidelengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm cannot exist.
We are thus able to see without construction why a triangle for the set of lengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm cannot exist. We have been able to figure this out through spatial intuition and reasoning.
Can we say anything about the existence of a triangle having sidelengths 3 cm, 3 cm and 7 cm? Verify your answer by construction.
In the rough diagram, is it possible to assign lengths in a different order such that the direct paths are always coming out to be shorter than the roundabout paths? If this is possible, then a triangle might exist. Is such rearrangement of lengths possible in the triangle?

lines: Can this understanding be used to tell something about the existence of a triangle having sidelengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm?

Let us suppose that there is a triangle for this set of lengths. Remember that at this point we are not sure about the existence of the triangle but we are only supposing that it exists. Let us draw a rough diagram.
If this triangle were possible, then the direct path between any two vertices should be shorter than the roundabout path via the third vertex. Is this true for our rough diagram?

Let us consider the paths between B and C. Direct path length = BC = 10 cm. Roundabout path length = BA + AC = 15 cm + 30 cm = 45 cm. Is the direct path length shorter than the roundabout path length? Yes.

Let us now consider the paths between A and B. Direct path length = AB = 15 cm. Roundabout path length = AC + CB = 30 cm + 10 cm = 40 cm. Is the direct path length shorter than the roundabout path length? Yes.

Finally, consider paths between C and A. Direct path length = CA = 30 cm. Roundabout path length = CB + BA = 10 cm + 15 cm = 25 cm. Is the direct path length shorter than the roundabout path length? In this case, the direct path is longer, which is absurd. Can such a triangle exist? No.
Therefore, a triangle having sidelengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm cannot exist.
We are thus able to see without construction why a triangle for the set of lengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm cannot exist. We have been able to figure this out through spatial intuition and reasoning.

1. Predict first: for 10, 15 and 30, is each length shorter than the other two added together?
2. Three comparisons are needed, one for each side as the direct path.
3. If even one comparison fails, no triangle exists. Moving the lengths to different sides of the rough figure does not help: the comparison 30 against 10 + 15 is the same wherever 30 is drawn.
4. For 3, 3 and 7: 7 is more than 3 + 3 = 6, so there is no triangle, and a construction with a base of 7 cm and arcs of 3 cm shows the arcs falling short.

content.text:
Worked example: Does a triangle exist with sidelengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm? Compare each direct length with the roundabout length.
1. Between B and C: direct BC = 10 cm; roundabout BA + AC = 15 + 30 = 45 cm. 10 < 45, which is fine.
2. Between A and B: direct AB = 15 cm; roundabout AC + CB = 30 + 10 = 40 cm. 15 < 40, which is fine.
3. Between C and A: direct CA = 30 cm; roundabout CB + BA = 10 + 15 = 25 cm. 30 > 25, which is absurd.
4. One direct path is longer than its roundabout path, so no triangle exists.
Answer: No triangle exists: 30 is greater than 10 + 15 = 25

concepts.concept_name: The triangle inequality: 10, 15, 30 and 3, 3, 7

content.text:
Worked example: Can we say anything about the existence of a triangle having sidelengths 3 cm, 3 cm and 7 cm? Verify by construction.
1. The longest length is 7 cm. The other two add to 3 + 3 = 6 cm.
2. 7 > 6, so the direct path of 7 cm is longer than the roundabout path of 6 cm. No triangle exists.
3. Check by construction: take the 7 cm side as the base and draw an arc of 3 cm from each end. The arcs cover 6 cm of the 7 cm and do not meet.
4. Rearranging the lengths does not help: 7 is still more than 3 + 3.
Answer: No triangle exists for 3, 3 and 7

concepts.concept_name: Practice: check lengths against the triangle inequality

content.text:
You would have realised that using a rough figure and comparing the direct path lengths with their corresponding roundabout path lengths is the same as comparing each length with the sum of the other two lengths. There are three such comparisons to be made.
Given three sidelengths, what do we need to compare to check for the existence of a triangle?
When each length is smaller than the sum of the other two, we say that the lengths satisfy the triangle inequality. For example, the set 3, 4, 5 satisfies the triangle inequality whereas, the set 10, 15, 30 does not satisfy the triangle inequality.
We have seen that lengths such as 10, 15, 30 that do not satisfy the triangle inequality cannot be the sidelengths of a triangle.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students try to construct triangles with sidelengths 3, 4, 8 and 2, 3, 6, see that the arcs do not meet, and look for more sets that fail.
Students compare a straight path with a path through a third point and state that the direct path is the shortest.
Students test lengths against the three direct-versus-roundabout comparisons and conclude that a triangle cannot exist when one comparison fails.
Students decide whether three lengths can make a triangle by comparing each length with the sum of the other two, and state the definition of satisfying the triangle inequality.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q1: We checked by construction that there are no triangles having sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm; and 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm. Check if you could have found this without trying to construct the triangle.
1. For 3, 4 and 8: the longest is 8 and the other two add to 3 + 4 = 7.
2. 8 > 7, so the direct length is longer than the roundabout length: no triangle.
3. For 2, 3 and 6: the longest is 6 and the other two add to 2 + 3 = 5.
4. 6 > 5, so again no triangle. No construction was needed.
Answer: Yes: 3 + 4 = 7 < 8 and 2 + 3 = 5 < 6, so neither set makes a triangle

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q2: Can we say anything about the existence of a triangle for each of the following sets of lengths? (a) 10 km, 10 km and 25 km (b) 5 mm, 10 mm and 20 mm (c) 12 cm, 20 cm and 40 cm
1. Compare the longest length with the sum of the other two; all three lengths in a set have the same unit.
2. (a) 10 + 10 = 20 and 20 < 25: no triangle.
3. (b) 5 + 10 = 15 and 15 < 20: no triangle.
4. (c) 12 + 20 = 32 and 32 < 40: no triangle.
Answer: No triangle exists in any of the three sets: (a) 20 < 25, (b) 15 < 20, (c) 32 < 40

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q3 (Try This)

content.text:
Figure it Out (the triangle inequality), Q3 (Try This): For the set 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm, two comparisons hold (10 < 15 + 30 and 15 < 10 + 30) but the third does not (30 > 10 + 15). Will there always be at least two comparisons where the direct length is less than the sum of the other two? Explore for different sets of lengths. Is it possible to tell which lengths will immediately be less than the sum of the other two, without calculations? [Hint: Consider the lengths in increasing order.]
1. Write the lengths in increasing order: a, b, c with a ≤ b ≤ c.
2. The length c is the longest, so a < b + c is true because b + c is already at least c, which is at least a. Also b < a + c, because a + c is at least c, which is at least b.
3. Only the comparison for c, c < a + b, can fail.
4. Test with 7, 10, 15: 7 < 10 + 15 = 25 and 10 < 7 + 15 = 22 hold, and the longest check 15 < 7 + 10 = 17 holds too. For 10, 15, 30 the first two hold and only the longest check, 30 < 25, fails.
5. So at least two comparisons always hold, and the two that always hold belong to the two shorter lengths. Only the longest length needs a check.
Answer: Yes, at least two comparisons always hold: the two shorter lengths are always less than the sum of the other two, so only the longest length needs to be checked

concepts.concept_name: Seeing the circles for 4, 5 and 8

content.text:
Does a triangle exist with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm?
This satisfies the triangle inequality: 8 < 4 + 5 = 9
This means that all the direct path lengths are less than the roundabout path lengths. Does this confirm the existence of a triangle?
If one of the direct path lengths had been longer, we could have concluded that a triangle would surely not exist. But in this case, we can only say that a triangle may or may not exist.
For the triangle to exist, the arcs that we construct to get the third vertex must intersect. Is it possible to determine that this will happen without actually carrying out the construction?
Visualising the construction of circles
Let us imagine that we start the construction by constructing the longest side as the base. Let AB be the base of length 8 cm. The next step is the construction of sufficiently long arcs corresponding to the other two lengths: 4 cm and 5 cm.
Instead of just constructing the arcs, let us complete the full circles. Suppose, we construct a circle of radius 4 cm with A as the centre. Now, suppose that a circle of radius 5 cm is constructed, centred at B. Can you draw a rough diagram of the resulting figure?
Note that in the figure below, AX = 4 cm and AB = 8 cm. So, what is BX? Does this length help in visualising the resulting figure?
Since BX = 4 cm, and the radius of the circle centred at B is 5 cm, it is clear that the circles will intersect each other at two points.
What does this tell us about the existence of a triangle? The points A and B along with either of the points of intersection of the circles will give us the required triangle. Thus, there exists a triangle having sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm.

1. Predict first: the circle at A reaches 4 cm along the base, and the circle at B has radius 5 cm. Does the circle at B reach past that point?
2. X is where the circle at A meets the base, so AX = 4 cm and BX = 8 − 4 = 4 cm.
3. The circle at B has radius 5 cm, which is more than BX = 4 cm, so the circle at B goes inside the circle at A and out again: the circles cross at two points.

content.text:
Worked example: Does a triangle exist with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm? Picture the circles on the longest side.
1. Check the longest length: 8 < 4 + 5 = 9, so the triangle inequality is satisfied.
2. Take the base AB = 8 cm. Draw a circle of radius 4 cm at A and a circle of radius 5 cm at B.
3. Let X be the point where the circle at A meets AB. Then AX = 4 cm, so BX = 8 − 4 = 4 cm.
4. BX = 4 cm is less than the radius 5 cm of the circle at B, so the circle at B goes beyond X, into the circle at A. The circles cross at two points.
5. Either crossing point with A and B gives a triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm.
Answer: Yes, a triangle exists with sidelengths 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm: the two circles cross at two points

content.text:

Worked example: Check the lengths 6, 7 and 12 by comparing only the longest length with the sum of the other two, and then check the other two comparisons to see that they hold.
1. The longest length is 12. The other two add to 6 + 7 = 13.
2. 12 < 13, so the longest comparison holds.
3. The other two comparisons: 6 < 7 + 12 = 19 and 7 < 6 + 12 = 18. Both hold, as they must, because 12 is already bigger than 6 and than 7.
4. All three hold, so the lengths satisfy the triangle inequality.

content.text:
Figure it Out (which lengths make a triangle), Q1: Which of the following lengths can be the sidelengths of a triangle? Explain your answers. Note that for each set, the three lengths have the same unit of measure. (a) 2, 2, 5 (b) 3, 4, 6 (c) 2, 4, 8 (d) 5, 5, 8 (e) 10, 20, 25 (f) 10, 20, 35 (g) 24, 26, 28
1. Compare the longest length with the sum of the other two.
2. (a) 2 + 2 = 4 < 5: no triangle. (b) 3 + 4 = 7 > 6: a triangle. (c) 2 + 4 = 6 < 8: no triangle.
3. (d) 5 + 5 = 10 > 8: a triangle. (e) 10 + 20 = 30 > 25: a triangle. (f) 10 + 20 = 30 < 35: no triangle.
4. (g) 24 + 26 = 50 > 28: a triangle.
Answer: Triangles exist for (b) 3, 4, 6; (d) 5, 5, 8; (e) 10, 20, 25; (g) 24, 26, 28. Not for (a), (c) or (f)

concepts.concept_name: Three cases for two circles

content.text:
Will triangles always exist when a set of lengths satisfies the triangle inequality? How can we be sure?
We can be sure of the existence of a triangle only if we can show that the circles intersect internally (as in Fig. 7.5) whenever the triangle inequality is satisfied. But are there other possibilities when the two circles are constructed? Let us visualise and study them.
The following different cases can be conceived: Case 1: Circles touch each other. Case 2: Circles do not intersect. Case 3: Circles intersect each other internally.
Note that while constructing the circles, we take (a) the length of the base AB = longest of the given length (b) the radii of the circles to be the smaller two lengths.
Which of the above-mentioned cases will lead to the formation of a triangle? Clearly, triangles are formed only when the circles intersect each other internally (Case 3).
Let us study each of these cases by finding the relation between the radii (the smaller two lengths) and AB (longest length).
Case 1: Circles touch each other at a point. For this case to happen, sum of the two radii = AB or sum of the two smaller lengths = longest length
Case 2: Circles do not intersect internally. For this case to happen, what should be the relation between the radii and AB? It can be seen from the figure that, sum of the two radii < AB or sum of the two smaller lengths < longest length
Case 3: Circles intersect each other. AB is composed of one radius and a part of the other. So, sum of the two radii > AB, or sum of the two smaller lengths > longest length

content.text:
1. Predict first: if the two radii add up to exactly the base, where do the circles meet?
2. Touch: the radii exactly fill the base, so the circles meet at one point on the base, and the three points are on one line. This is the answer to the question of three vertices on a line.
3. Miss: the radii add up to less than the base, so a gap is left between the circles.
4. Cross: the radii add up to more than the base, so the circles overlap and meet at two points.

content.text:
Worked example: On a base AB, take two circles whose radii are the two smaller lengths. For the sets 3, 5, 8 and 2, 5, 8 and 5, 6, 8 say whether the circles touch, miss or cross, and whether a triangle exists.
1. 3, 5, 8: the base is 8 and the radii are 3 and 5. The radii add to 3 + 5 = 8, equal to the base, so the circles touch at one point. No triangle.
2. 2, 5, 8: the radii add to 2 + 5 = 7, less than 8, so the circles miss. No triangle.
3. 5, 6, 8: the radii add to 5 + 6 = 11, more than 8, so the circles cross in two points. A triangle exists.
Answer: 3, 5, 8: touch, no triangle; 2, 5, 8: miss, no triangle; 5, 6, 8: cross, a triangle exists

concepts.concept_name: A complete test for a triangle

content.text:
Can we use this analysis to tell if a triangle exists when the lengths satisfy the triangle inequality?
If the given lengths satisfy the triangle inequality, then the sum of the two smaller lengths is greater than the longest length. This means that this will lead to Case 3 where the circles intersect internally, and so a triangle exists.
How will the two circles turn out for a set of lengths that do not satisfy the triangle inequality? Find 3 examples of sets of lengths for which the circles: (a) touch each other at a point, (b) do not intersect.
Frame a complete procedure that can be used to check the existence of a triangle.
Conclusion: If a given set of three lengths satisfies the triangle inequality, then a triangle exists having those as sidelengths. If the set does not satisfy the triangle inequality, then a triangle with those sidelengths does not exist.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if the lengths satisfy the triangle inequality, which of the three cases happens?
2. The inequality says the two smaller lengths add to more than the longest, which is Case 3: the circles cross and a triangle exists.
3. If the inequality fails, the sum is equal to the longest length (the circles touch) or less (the circles miss): no triangle either way.
4. Touching examples: 2, 3, 5; 4, 4, 8; 1, 6, 7. Missing examples: 1, 2, 5; 3, 3, 9; 2, 4, 10.

content.text:
Worked example: Frame a complete procedure to check whether three lengths can make a triangle, and use it on 3.5, 6 and 9, and on 4, 7 and 11.
1. Step 1: find the longest length.
2. Step 2: add the other two lengths.
3. Step 3: if the sum is more than the longest, a triangle exists; if the sum is equal or less, it does not.
4. 3.5, 6, 9: the longest is 9 and 3.5 + 6 = 9.5. 9.5 > 9, so a triangle exists.
5. 4, 7, 11: the longest is 11 and 4 + 7 = 11. The sum equals the longest, so the circles touch and no triangle exists.
Answer: A triangle exists for 3.5, 6 and 9; none exists for 4, 7 and 11

Students conclude that a triangle exists exactly when the longest length is less than the sum of the other two, find sets that give touching or missing circles, and write a procedure.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q1: Check if a triangle exists for each of the following set of lengths: (a) 1, 100, 100 (b) 3, 6, 9 (c) 1, 1, 5 (d) 5, 10, 12
1. (a) The longest is 100 and 1 + 100 = 101 > 100: a triangle exists.
2. (b) The longest is 9 and 3 + 6 = 9, equal to 9: the circles touch, so no triangle.
3. (c) The longest is 5 and 1 + 1 = 2 < 5: no triangle.
4. (d) The longest is 12 and 5 + 10 = 15 > 12: a triangle exists.
Answer: Triangles exist for (a) and (d); not for (b) (circles touch) or (c)

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q2: Does there exist an equilateral triangle with sides 50, 50, 50? In general, does there exist an equilateral triangle of any sidelength? Justify your answer.
1. For 50, 50, 50 the longest is 50 and the other two add to 50 + 50 = 100.
2. 50 < 100, so the triangle inequality holds and an equilateral triangle exists.
3. For any side length s the other two add to s + s = 2s, and s < 2s as long as s is more than zero.
4. So the circles always cross: an equilateral triangle exists for every side length. It can be built with the two-arcs method of the first topic.
Answer: Yes: 50 < 50 + 50, and in general s < s + s for any side length s above zero

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q3 (Try This)

content.text:
Figure it Out (circles and the third length), Q3 (Try This): For each of the following, give at least 5 possible values for the third length so there exists a triangle having these as sidelengths (decimal values could also be chosen): (a) 1, 100 (b) 5, 5 (c) 3, 7. See if you can describe all possible lengths of the third side in each case, so that a triangle exists with those sidelengths. For example, in case (a), all numbers strictly between 99 and 101 would be possible.
1. The third length x must be less than the sum of the other two, and the other two lengths must each be less than the sum of x and the remaining length.
2. (a) 1 and 100: x < 1 + 100 = 101, and 100 < 1 + x gives x > 99. So x is strictly between 99 and 101: for example 99.5, 100, 100.5, 99.9 and 100.9.
3. (b) 5 and 5: x < 5 + 5 = 10, and 5 < 5 + x gives x > 0. So x is strictly between 0 and 10: for example 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9.
4. (c) 3 and 7: x < 3 + 7 = 10, and 7 < 3 + x gives x > 4. So x is strictly between 4 and 10: for example 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9.
5. In general, for two lengths p and q, the third length is strictly between the difference of p and q and the sum of p and q.
Answer: (a) strictly between 99 and 101, for example 99.5, 100, 100.5; (b) strictly between 0 and 10, for example 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; (c) strictly between 4 and 10, for example 5, 6, 7, 8, 9

video_script.substitution: The side length is fifty, and then any side length greater than zero.
video_script.anchor: Three equal sides of fifty, with the other two added together
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, an equilateral triangle exists for fifty, and for every side length.

final_answer.value: Yes: 50 < 50 + 50, and in general s < s + s for any side length s above zero
final_answer.spoken: yes, an equilateral triangle exists for fifty, and for every side length

maths_rules: 50, 50, 50: longest 50; other two 50 + 50 = 100; 50 < 100, passes
any side length s > 0: other two s + s = 2s; s < 2s, passes

concepts.concept_name: The included angle

content.text:
7.3 Construction of Triangles When Some Sides and Angles are Given
We have seen how to construct triangles when their sidelengths are given. Now, we will take up constructions where in place of some sidelengths, angle measures are given.
Two Sides and the Included Angle
How do we construct a triangle if two sides and the angle included between them are given? Here are some examples of measurements showing the included angle.
4 cm, 60°, 3 cm; 5 cm, 30°, 6 cm; 2 cm, 40°, 3 cm

We have seen how to construct triangles when their sidelengths are given. Now, we will take up constructions where in place of some sidelengths, angle measures are given.
Two Sides and the Included Angle

content.text:
1. Predict first: in the set 4 cm, 60°, 3 cm, which two sides does the 60° angle sit between?
2. The included angle is the angle between the two given sides, where those two sides meet at a vertex.
3. The three examples are: 4 cm, 60°, 3 cm; 5 cm, 30°, 6 cm; and 2 cm, 40°, 3 cm.

steps: Predict first: in the set 4 cm, 60°, 3 cm, which two sides does the 60° angle sit between?
The included angle is the angle between the two given sides, where those two sides meet at a vertex.
The three examples are: 4 cm, 60°, 3 cm; 5 cm, 30°, 6 cm; and 2 cm, 40°, 3 cm.

content.text:
Worked example: A triangle has two sides of 6 cm and 5 cm that meet at a corner, and the angle at that corner is 30°. Is 30° the included angle? What if the 30° angle were at the other end of the 6 cm side?
1. The two given sides, 6 cm and 5 cm, meet at one corner. The angle at that corner is between them, so 30° is the included angle.
2. If the 30° angle were at the other end of the 6 cm side, one of its arms would be the 6 cm side but the other arm would be a side that is not given.
3. That angle is not between the two given sides, so it is not the included angle. The measurements would then be a different kind of data.
Answer: Yes, 30° is included when it sits between the 6 cm and 5 cm sides; at the other end it is not

concepts.concept_name: Constructing 5 cm, 45° and 4 cm

content.text:
Construct a triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, AC = 4 cm and ∠A = 45°.
Let us take one of the given sides, AB, as the base of the triangle.
Step 1: Construct a side AB of length 5 cm.
Step 2: Construct ∠A = 45° by drawing the other arm of the angle.
Step 3: Mark the point C on the other arm such that AC = 4 cm.
Step 4: Join BC to get the required triangle.

1. Predict first: after AB and the 45° arm are drawn, is C anywhere on the arm, or at one exact place?
2. C is at one exact place: 4 cm from A along the arm. Joining BC then closes the triangle, and BC comes out at about 3.6 cm.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, AC = 4 cm and ∠A = 45°.
1. Step 1: draw the base AB = 5 cm.
2. Step 2: place the protractor at A and mark 45° from AB. Draw a long arm through the mark.
3. Step 3: with the ruler or compass measure 4 cm from A along the arm and mark the point C.
4. Step 4: join BC.
5. Measuring BC gives about 3.6 cm, so the sides are 5 cm, 4 cm and about 3.6 cm.
Answer: Triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, AC = 4 cm, ∠A = 45° and BC about 3.6 cm

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (two sides and the included angle), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (two sides and the included angle), Q1: Construct triangles for the following measurements where the angle is included between the sides: (a) 3 cm, 75°, 7 cm (b) 6 cm, 25°, 3 cm (c) 3 cm, 120°, 8 cm
1. Use the same four steps each time: draw the first side as the base, make the angle at one end, mark the second side along the new arm, and join.
2. (a) AB = 3 cm, ∠A = 75°, AC = 7 cm. Joining BC gives a third side of about 6.9 cm.
3. (b) AB = 6 cm, ∠A = 25°, AC = 3 cm. The third side is about 3.5 cm, and the triangle is thin because the angle is small.
4. (c) AB = 3 cm, ∠A = 120°, AC = 8 cm. The angle is obtuse, and the third side is about 9.8 cm.
Answer: (a) third side about 6.9 cm, (b) about 3.5 cm, (c) about 9.8 cm; all three triangles can be built

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (two sides and the included angle), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (two sides and the included angle), Q2: We have seen that triangles do not exist for all sets of sidelengths. Is there a combination of measurements in the case of two sides and the included angle where a triangle is not possible? Justify your answer using what you observe during construction.
1. Draw the base and the arm for the angle, then mark the second side along the arm.
2. If the angle is 180° the arm points straight along the base, away from it, so the two sides lie on one line and joining the ends gives no triangle. Examples: 3 cm, 180°, 7 cm.
3. If the angle is more than 180°, for example 4 cm, 210°, 6 cm, the angle on the other side is less than 180° and the picture is the same as a smaller angle; a measure of 180° or more cannot be the angle of a triangle.
4. An angle of 0° puts the arm on top of the base, so there is no triangle either.
5. For every angle strictly between 0° and 180° the free ends can be joined, so a triangle always exists.
Answer: Yes: no triangle when the included angle is 180° or more (for example 3 cm, 180°, 7 cm or 4 cm, 210°, 6 cm), or 0°; for any angle strictly between 0° and 180° a triangle exists

maths_rules: with the angle 180° the arm points straight out along the base line, so A, B and C lie on one straight line and there is no triangle

concepts.concept_name: Constructing 45°, 5 cm and 80°

content.text:
Two Angles and the Included Side
In this case, we are given two angles and the side that is a part of both angles, which we call the included side. Here are some examples of such measurements:
40°, 5 cm, 50°; 30°, 4 cm, 45°; 20°, 6 cm, 50°
Construct a triangle ABC where AB = 5 cm, ∠A = 45° and ∠B = 80°.
Let us take the given side as the base.
Step 1: Draw the base AB of length 5 cm.
Step 2: Draw ∠A and ∠B of measures 45°, and 80° respectively.
Step 3: The point of intersection of the two new line segments is the third vertex C.

content.text:
1. Predict first: the 5 cm side has an angle at each end. Where will the two new arms meet?
2. The included side is the side that is a part of both angles. In 40°, 5 cm, 50° it is the 5 cm side.
3. The point where the two arms cross is C. It is the only point that is on both arms, so the triangle is fixed: AC is about 6.0 cm and BC about 4.3 cm.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a triangle ABC where AB = 5 cm, ∠A = 45° and ∠B = 80°.
1. Step 1: draw the base AB = 5 cm. It is the side that both angles share, the included side.
2. Step 2: at A make an angle of 45° and draw a long arm. At B make an angle of 80° on the same side and draw a long arm.
3. Step 3: the two arms cross at C, the third vertex.
4. Measuring gives AC about 6.0 cm and BC about 4.3 cm, and the angle at C is 180° − 45° − 80° = 55°.
Answer: Triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, ∠A = 45°, ∠B = 80°, AC about 6.0 cm, BC about 4.3 cm

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (two angles and the included side), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (two angles and the included side), Q1: Construct triangles for the following measurements: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75° (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60° (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°
1. Draw the given side as the base. Make the first angle at one end and the second at the other end. The arms cross at the third vertex.
2. (a) 75° + 75° = 150° < 180°, so the arms cross; the third angle is 30° and the other two sides are each about 9.7 cm.
3. (b) 25° + 60° = 85° < 180°; the third angle is 95° and the other two sides are about 2.6 cm and 1.3 cm.
4. (c) 120° + 30° = 150° < 180°; the third angle is 30° and the other two sides are about 10.4 cm and 6 cm.
Answer: All three triangles can be built: (a) third angle 30°, (b) third angle 95°, (c) third angle 30°

concepts.concept_name: Two big angles never meet

content.text:
Do triangles always exist?
Do triangles exist for every combination of two angles and their included side? Explore.
As in the case when we are given all three sides, it turns out that there is not always a triangle for every combination of two angles and the included side.
Find examples of measurements of two angles with the included side where a triangle is not possible.
Let us try to visualise such a situation. Once the base is drawn, try to imagine how the other sides should be so that they do not meet.
Here are some obvious examples.
If the two angles are greater than or equal to a right angle (90°), then it is clear that a triangle is not possible.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if both base angles are 90°, will the two arms ever meet?
2. At 90° the arms stand straight up from the base and stay the same distance apart, so they never meet. When the angles are bigger than 90°, the arms lean away from each other and spread out.
3. So two angles that are each 90° or more cannot be the base angles of a triangle, whatever the length of the base.

content.text:
Worked example: Say why no triangle can be built from the angles 90°, 5 cm, 90°, and from 100°, 5 cm, 95°.
1. Draw the base of 5 cm.
2. With 90° at both ends the arms are straight up from the base, side by side. They never meet.
3. With 100° and 95° the arms lean outwards from the base, so they get further apart. They never meet.
4. Two angles that are each 90° or more always give arms that do not meet.
Answer: No triangle: arms at 90° or more do not meet

concepts.concept_name: A 40° angle, and the line that never meets

content.text:
Now we make one of the base angles an acute angle, say 40°. What are the possible values that the other angle should take so that the lines don't meet?
It is clear that if the line from B is 'inclined' sufficiently to the right, then it will not meet the line l.
(a) Try to find a possible ∠B (marked in the figure) for this to happen.
(b) What could be smallest value of ∠B for the lines to not meet?
The blue line is the line with the least rightward bend that doesn't meet the line 'l'
Visually, it is clear that the line that creates the smallest ∠B has to be the one parallel to l. Let us call this parallel line m.
Can you tell the actual value of ∠B be in this case? [Hint: Note that AB is the transversal.]
We have seen that when two lines are parallel, the internal angles on the same side of the transversal add up to 180°. So ∠B = 140°.
So, for what values of ∠B, does a triangle not exist? Does the length AB play any part here?
From the discussion above, it can be seen that the length AB does not play any part in deciding the existence of a triangle. We can say that a triangle does not exist when ∠B is greater than or equal to 140°.

content.text:
1. Predict first: with ∠A = 40°, if the line from B leans a lot to the right, does it meet the line l?
2. The line that leans the least and still never meets l is the line m parallel to l. It makes the smallest angle B that fails.
3. AB is a transversal of the parallel lines l and m, and the angles on the same side add to 180°: ∠B = 180° − 40° = 140°.
4. For ∠B less than 140° the line from B meets l and a triangle exists. For ∠B of 140° or more it does not. The length of AB was never used.

content.text:
Worked example: The angle at A is 40°. Find the smallest angle at B for which the arms from A and B do not meet, and say whether the length AB matters.
1. Draw AB and the arm from A at 40°. Call the line along this arm l.
2. The arm from B that does not meet l and leans the least is the line m parallel to l.
3. AB is a transversal of the parallel lines l and m. The angles on the same side add to 180°.
4. So ∠B = 180° − 40° = 140°.
5. Any ∠B of 140° or more does not meet l; any ∠B less than 140° does. The length of AB is not used anywhere.
Answer: ∠B = 140°: no triangle when ∠B is 140° or more; the length of AB does not matter

concepts.concept_name: Practice: which pairs of angles can make a triangle

content.text:
Like the triangle inequality, can you form a rule that describes the two angles for which a triangle is possible?
When the sum of two given angles is less than 180°, a triangle exists with these angles. If the sum is greater than or equal to 180°, there is no triangle with these angles.

content.text:
Two angles can be the angles of a triangle exactly when they add up to less than 180°.
For a given angle, the other angle must be less than 180° minus the given angle.
The length of the side between the angles does not matter.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (when two angles fail), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (when two angles fail), Q1: For each of the following angles, find another angle for which a triangle is (a) possible, (b) not possible. Find at least two different angles for each category: (i) 30° (ii) 70° (iii) 54° (iv) 144°
1. The other angle must be less than 180° minus the given angle; at that value or more the arms do not meet.
2. (i) 30°: possible if the other angle is less than 150°, for example 40° or 100°; not possible for 150° or more, for example 150° or 170°.
3. (ii) 70°: possible below 110°, for example 20° or 100°; not possible at 110° or more, for example 110° or 130°.
4. (iii) 54°: possible below 126°, for example 30° or 120°; not possible at 126° or more, for example 126° or 150°.
5. (iv) 144°: possible below 36°, for example 10° or 30°; not possible at 36° or more, for example 36° or 90°.
Answer: (i) 30°: possible 40°, 100°; not possible 150°, 170°. (ii) 70°: possible 20°, 100°; not possible 110°, 130°. (iii) 54°: possible 30°, 120°; not possible 126°, 150°. (iv) 144°: possible 10°, 30°; not possible 36°, 90°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (when two angles fail), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (when two angles fail), Q2: Determine which of the following pairs can be the angles of a triangle and which cannot: (a) 35°, 150° (b) 70°, 30° (c) 90°, 85° (d) 50°, 150°
1. Add the two angles. If the sum is less than 180° the arms meet; if it is 180° or more they do not.
2. (a) 35° + 150° = 185° is more than 180°: cannot.
3. (b) 70° + 30° = 100° is less than 180°: can.
4. (c) 90° + 85° = 175° is less than 180°: can.
5. (d) 50° + 150° = 200° is more than 180°: cannot.
Answer: (b) and (c) can be the angles of a triangle; (a) and (d) cannot

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (when two angles fail), Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out (when two angles fail), Q3: Like the triangle inequality, can you form a rule that describes the two angles for which a triangle is possible? Can the sum of the two angles be used for framing this rule?
1. Take the pairs from the last question: the pairs that work, 70° and 30°, and 90° and 85°, add up to 100° and 175°. The pairs that fail add up to 185° and 200°.
2. For a first angle of 40° the second angle fails from 140° on, and 40° + 140° = 180°.
3. So the sum decides it: when the sum of the two angles is less than 180°, a triangle exists. When the sum is 180° or more, there is no triangle.
4. Each angle must also be more than 0°.
Answer: A triangle exists when the two angles are each more than 0° and their sum is less than 180°; if the sum is 180° or more there is no triangle

concepts.concept_name: The same angles with a longer side

content.text:
Let us take two angles, say 60° and 70°, whose sum is less than 180°. Let the included side be 5 cm.
What could the measure of the third angle be? Does this measure change if the base length is changed to some other value, say 7 cm? Construct and find out.
In general, once the two angles are fixed, does the third angle depend on the included sidelength? Try with different pairs of angles and lengths.
The measurements might show that the sidelength has no effect (or a very small effect) on the third angle. With this observation, let us see if we can find the third angle without carrying out the construction and measurement.
Try experimenting with different triangles to see if there is a relation between any two angles and the third one. To find this relation, what data will you keep track of and how will you organise the data you collect?

1. Predict first: if the base is longer, will the third angle be bigger, smaller or the same?
2. With 60° and 70° the third angle measures 50° for a base of 5 cm and also for a base of 7 cm: the longer base makes the whole triangle bigger, but the angles stay the same.

content.text:
Worked example: Build a triangle with angles 60° and 70° at the ends of a base of 5 cm, then one with a base of 7 cm, and compare the third angle.
1. Base 5 cm: arms at 60° and 70° cross at C. The angle at C measures 50°.
2. Base 7 cm: arms at 60° and 70° cross at C. The angle at C still measures 50°.
3. The triangle with the longer base is a bigger copy, with every length scaled up but the same angles.
4. In both triangles 60° + 70° + 50° = 180°. The third angle is decided by the two given angles alone.
Answer: The third angle is 50° for both bases; it does not depend on the length of the side

concepts.concept_name: A parallel line through the top vertex

content.text:
Consider a triangle ABC with ∠B = 50° and ∠C = 70°. Let us see how we can find ∠A without construction.
We saw that the notion of parallel lines was useful to determine that the sum of any two angles of a triangle is less than 180°. Parallel lines can be used to find the third angle, ∠BAC as well.
Let us suppose we construct a line XY parallel to BC through vertex A. We can see new angles being formed here: ∠XAB, and ∠YAC. What are their values?
Since the line XY is parallel to BC, ∠XAB = ∠B and ∠YAC = ∠C, because they are alternate angles of the transversals AB and AC.
Therefore, ∠XAB = 50°, and ∠YAC = 70°. Can we find ∠BAC from this?
We know that ∠XAB, ∠YAC and ∠BAC together form 180°. So ∠XAB + ∠YAC + ∠BAC = 180°, 50° + ∠BAC + 70° = 180°, 120° + ∠BAC = 180°. Thus, ∠BAC = 60°
Now construct a triangle (taking BC to be of any suitable length) and verify if this is indeed the case.

Let us suppose we construct a line XY parallel to BC through vertex A. We can see new angles being formed here: ∠XAB, and ∠YAC. What are their values?
Since the line XY is parallel to BC, ∠XAB = ∠B and ∠YAC = ∠C, because they are alternate angles of the transversals AB and AC.
Therefore, ∠XAB = 50°, and ∠YAC = 70°. Can we find ∠BAC from this?
We know that ∠XAB, ∠YAC and ∠BAC together form 180°. So ∠XAB + ∠YAC + ∠BAC = 180°, 50° + ∠BAC + 70° = 180°, 120° + ∠BAC = 180°. Thus, ∠BAC = 60°
Now construct a triangle (taking BC to be of any suitable length) and verify if this is indeed the case.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (finding the third angle), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (finding the third angle), Q1: Find the third angle of a triangle (using a parallel line) when two of the angles are: (a) 36°, 72° (b) 150°, 15° (c) 90°, 30° (d) 75°, 45°
1. Draw a line through the third vertex parallel to the side between the two given angles; its two alternate angles are equal to the two given angles.
2. The third angle is what remains of 180°.
3. (a) 180° − 36° − 72° = 72°. (b) 180° − 150° − 15° = 15°.
4. (c) 180° − 90° − 30° = 60°. (d) 180° − 75° − 45° = 60°.
Answer: (a) 72° (b) 15° (c) 60° (d) 60°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (finding the third angle), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (finding the third angle), Q2: Can you construct a triangle all of whose angles are equal to 70°? If two of the angles are 70° what would the third angle be? If all the angles in a triangle have to be equal, then what must its measure be? Explore and find out.
1. Three angles of 70° add up to 3 × 70° = 210°, which is more than 180°. So no triangle has all angles equal to 70°.
2. If two angles are 70°, the third is 180° − 70° − 70° = 40°.
3. If all three angles are equal and each is x, then 3x = 180°, so x = 60°.
Answer: No triangle has three angles of 70°; two angles of 70° give a third of 40°; equal angles must each be 60°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (finding the third angle), Q3 (Try This)

content.text:
Figure it Out (finding the third angle), Q3 (Try This): Here is a triangle in which we know ∠B = ∠C and ∠A = 50°. Can you find ∠B and ∠C?
1. The three angles add up to 180°, so ∠B + ∠C = 180° − 50° = 130°.
2. ∠B and ∠C are equal, so each is half of 130°.
3. 130° ÷ 2 = 65°.
Answer: ∠B = ∠C = 65°

concepts.concept_name: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°

content.text:
Angle Sum Property
What can we say about the sum of the angles of any triangle?
Consider a triangle ABC. To find the sum of its angles, we can use the same method of drawing a line parallel to the base: construct a line through A that is parallel to BC.
We need to find ∠A + ∠B + ∠C. We know that ∠B = ∠XAB, ∠C = ∠YAC. So, ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = ∠A + ∠XAB + ∠YAC = 180° as together they form a straight angle.
Thus we have proved that the sum of the three angles in any triangle is 180°! This rather surprising result is called the angle sum property of triangles.
Take some time to reflect upon how we figured out the angle sum property. In the beginning, the relationship between the third angle and the other two angles was not at all clear. However, a simple idea of drawing a line parallel to the base through the top vertex suddenly made the relationship obvious. This ingenious idea can be found in a very influential book in the history of mathematics called 'The Elements'. This book is attributed to the Greek mathematician Euclid, who lived around 300 BCE.
This solution is yet another example of how creative thinking plays a key role in mathematics!
There is a convenient way of verifying the angle sum property by folding a triangular cut-out of a paper. Do you see how this shows that the sum of the angles in this triangle is 180°?

content.text:
Worked example: Prove that the three angles of a triangle ABC add up to 180°, and check it with the paper fold.
1. Draw a line XY through A parallel to BC.
2. Alternate angles give ∠XAB = ∠B and ∠YAC = ∠C.
3. ∠XAB, ∠A and ∠YAC together make a straight angle: ∠XAB + ∠A + ∠YAC = 180°.
4. Replace ∠XAB by ∠B and ∠YAC by ∠C: ∠B + ∠A + ∠C = 180°.
5. Paper fold: fold the three corners of a paper triangle in so that they meet at one point on the base. The three angles sit side by side along the straight base, which is 180°.
Answer: ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180° for every triangle

concepts.concept_name: Exterior angles

content.text:
Exterior Angles
The angle formed between the extension of a side of a triangle and the other side is called an exterior angle of the triangle. In this figure, ∠ACD is an exterior angle.
Find ∠ACD, if ∠A = 50°, and ∠B = 60°.
From the angle sum property, we know that 50° + 60° + ∠ACB = 180°. 110° + ∠ACB = 180°. So, ∠ACB = 70°. So, ∠ACD = 180° − 70° = 110°, since, ∠ACB and ∠ACD together form a straight angle.
Find the exterior angle for different measures of ∠A and ∠B. Do you see any relation between the exterior angle and these two angles?
[Hint: From angle sum property, we have ∠A + ∠B + ∠ACB = 180°.] We also have ∠ACD + ∠ACB = 180°, since they form a straight angle. What does this show?

content.text:
1. Predict first: if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°, is the exterior angle at C more or less than 100°?
2. From the angle sum property ∠ACB = 70°, and ∠ACD = 180° − 70° = 110°.
3. Since ∠A + ∠B + ∠ACB = 180° and ∠ACD + ∠ACB = 180°, the two sums are equal, and taking away ∠ACB from both leaves ∠ACD = ∠A + ∠B.
4. Check: 50° + 60° = 110°. The exterior angle is the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it.

content.text:
Worked example: Find ∠ACD, if ∠A = 50° and ∠B = 60°, and then try ∠A = 35° and ∠B = 45°. What do you notice?
1. First case: 50° + 60° + ∠ACB = 180°, so ∠ACB = 70°.
2. ∠ACB and ∠ACD form a straight angle, so ∠ACD = 180° − 70° = 110°.
3. Second case: 35° + 45° + ∠ACB = 180°, so ∠ACB = 100°, and ∠ACD = 180° − 100° = 80°.
4. In the first case 110° = 50° + 60°; in the second case 80° = 35° + 45°.
5. The exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it.
Answer: ∠ACD = 110°, and in general an exterior angle is the sum of the two opposite interior angles

media.context: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How is the angle outside a triangle linked to the inside?
items: The angle formed between the extension of a side of a triangle and the other side is called an exterior angle of the triangle. In this figure, ∠ACD is an exterior angle. Find ∠ACD, if ∠A = 50°, and ∠B = 60°. From the angle sum property, we know that 50° + 60° + ∠ACB = 180°, so ∠ACB = 70°. So, ∠ACD = 180° - 70° = 110°, since ∠ACB and ∠ACD together form a straight angle. Find the exterior angle for different measures of ∠A and ∠B. Do you see any relation between the exterior angle and these two angles?

concepts.concept_name: Height and altitude

content.text:
7.4 Constructions Related to Altitudes of Triangles
There is another set of useful measurements with respect to a triangle, the height of each of its vertices with respect to the opposite sides.
In the world around us, we talk of the heights of various objects: the height of a person, the height of a tree, the height of a building, etc. What do we mean by the word 'height'?
Consider a triangle ABC. What is the height of the vertex A from its opposite side BC, and how can it be measured?
Let AD be the line segment from A drawn perpendicular to BC. The length of AD is the height of the vertex A from BC. The line segment AD is said to be one of the 'altitudes' of the triangle. The other altitudes are BE and CF in the figure below: the perpendiculars drawn from the other vertices to their respective opposite sides.
Whenever we use the word height of the triangle, we generally refer to the length of the altitude to whatever side we take as base (this altitude is AD in the case of Fig. 7.8).
Construction of the Altitudes of a Triangle
Construct an arbitrary triangle. Label the vertices A, B, C taking BC to be the base.
Construct the altitude from A to BC.
Constructing the altitude using just a ruler is not accurate. To get a more precise angle of 90°, we use a set square along with a ruler. Can you see how to do this?
Step 1: Keep the ruler aligned to the base. Place the set square on the ruler as shown, such that one of the edges of the right angle touches the ruler.
Step 2: Slide the set square along the ruler till the vertical edge of the set square touches the vertex A.
Step 3: Draw the altitude to BC through A using the vertical edge of the set square.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a triangle has three corners. How many altitudes does it have?
2. The height of a vertex from the opposite side is the length of the perpendicular from the vertex to that side. The perpendicular segment is called an altitude, and every triangle has three, one from each vertex.
3. Height of the triangle usually means the length of the altitude to the side taken as the base.
4. A ruler alone is not accurate for a right angle, so use a set square: slide it along the base until its upright edge touches the vertex, then draw along that edge.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw the altitude from A to the base BC of a triangle ABC using a ruler and a set square.
1. Step 1: keep the ruler along the base BC, and place the set square on the ruler with one edge of its right angle against the ruler.
2. Step 2: slide the set square along the ruler until its upright edge touches A.
3. Step 3: draw along the upright edge from A down to BC. This segment AD is the altitude.
4. AD is perpendicular to BC, so the angle at D is 90°, and the length of AD is the height of A from BC.
Answer: AD, the perpendicular from A to BC, is the altitude from A; its length is the height

content.text:
1. Predict first: in a triangle with a very wide angle at B, where does the perpendicular from A land?
2. It lands outside the triangle. Extend the base BC beyond B and drop the perpendicular from A to this extended line.
3. Paper fold: fold the paper so that the base folds onto itself and the crease passes through the top vertex. The two parts of the base line match, so the two angles made by the crease are equal, and they make a straight angle of 180°. Each is therefore 90°, so the crease is perpendicular.

content.text:
Worked example: In triangle ABC the angle at B is obtuse. Draw the altitude from A to BC and say where it lies.
1. Extend the base BC beyond B into a longer line.
2. Slide the set square along the extended line until its upright edge touches A.
3. Draw the perpendicular from A to the extended line. The foot D is on the extension, outside the triangle.
4. So an altitude can lie outside the triangle.
5. Paper fold check: fold so that the base falls on itself with the crease through A. The two angles at the crease are equal and add up to 180°, so each is 90°.
Answer: The altitude from A meets the extended base outside the triangle; the paper crease is perpendicular because its two equal angles add up to 180°

content.text:
Does there exist a triangle in which a side is also an altitude? Visualise such a triangle and draw a rough diagram.
We see that this happens in triangles where one of the angles is a right angle.
Triangles having one right angle are called right-angled triangles or simply right triangles.

2. In a triangle with a right angle at B, the side AB is perpendicular to BC. So AB is the altitude from A to BC, and BC is the altitude from C to AB.
3. A triangle with one right angle is called a right-angled triangle, or a right triangle.

content.text:
Worked example: In a triangle ABC with a right angle at B, name two altitudes that are also sides.
1. AB meets BC at 90°. The perpendicular from A to BC is AB itself, so AB is the altitude from A.
2. In the same way BC meets AB at 90°, so BC is the altitude from C to AB.
3. The altitude from B goes to the long side AC and lies inside the triangle.
Answer: AB and BC are both sides and altitudes in a right-angled triangle with the right angle at B

source_video_walkthrough.title: How do we draw the height of a corner of a triangle?
items: Let AD be the line segment from A drawn perpendicular to BC. The length of AD is the height of the vertex A from BC. The line segment AD is said to be one of the altitudes of the triangle. Construct the altitude from A to BC. Constructing the altitude using just a ruler is not accurate. To get a more precise angle of 90°, we use a set square along with a ruler. Step 1: Keep the ruler aligned to the base. Place the set square on the ruler as shown, such that one of the edges of the right angle touches the ruler. Step 2: Slide the set square along the ruler till the vertical edge of the set square touches the vertex A. Step 3: Draw the altitude to BC through A using the vertical edge of the set square.

concepts.concept_name: Sorting triangles by their sides

content.text:
7.5 Types of Triangles
In our study of triangles, we have encountered the following types of triangles; equilateral, isosceles, scalene and right-angled triangles. Did you spot any other type of triangle?
The classification of triangles as equilateral and isosceles was based on equality of sides.
Equilateral triangles have sides of equal length. Isosceles triangles have two sides of equal length. Scalene triangles have sides of three different lengths.
Can a similar classification be done based on equality of angles? Is there any relation between these two classifications? We will answer these questions in a later chapter.

2. Equilateral means all three sides are equal, isosceles means two sides are equal, and scalene means all three sides are different.
3. Whether equal angles go with equal sides is answered in a later chapter.

content.text:
Worked example: Name the kind of triangle with sides (a) 5 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm (b) 5 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm (c) 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm, after checking each really is a triangle.
1. Check each with the triangle inequality: 5 < 5 + 5; 8 < 5 + 5; 7 < 5 + 6. All three exist.
2. (a) All three sides are equal: equilateral.
3. (b) Exactly two sides are equal: isosceles.
4. (c) All three sides are different: scalene.
Answer: (a) equilateral (b) isosceles (c) scalene

concepts.concept_name: Sorting triangles by their angles

content.text:
We used angle measures when classifying a triangle as a right-angled triangle. What are the other types of triangles based on angle measures?
A classification of triangles based on their angle measures is acute-angled, right-angled and obtuse-angled. We have already seen what a right-angled triangle is. It is a triangle with one right angle. Similarly, an obtuse-angled triangle has one obtuse angle.
What could an acute-angled triangle be? Can we define it as a triangle with one acute angle? Why not?
In an acute-angled triangle, all three angles are acute angles.

lines: We used angle measures when classifying a triangle as a right-angled triangle. What are the other types of triangles based on angle measures?

A classification of triangles based on their angle measures is acute-angled, right-angled and obtuse-angled. We have already seen what a right-angled triangle is. It is a triangle with one right angle. Similarly, an obtuse-angled triangle has one obtuse angle.
What could an acute-angled triangle be? Can we define it as a triangle with one acute angle? Why not?
In an acute-angled triangle, all three angles are acute angles.

content.text:
1. Predict first: can a triangle have two obtuse angles? Think about the angle sum.
2. A right-angled triangle has one right angle, and an obtuse-angled triangle has one obtuse angle. Two such angles already use up 180° or more, so a triangle never has two of them.
3. Can an acute-angled triangle be one with one acute angle? No: every triangle has at least two acute angles, because the other two angles can be 90° and more only once. A triangle with angles 90°, 50°, 40° has acute angles and is still right-angled.
4. So an acute-angled triangle has all three angles acute.

content.text:
Worked example: Name the kind of triangle with angles (a) 50°, 60°, 70° (b) 90°, 50°, 40° (c) 120°, 30°, 30°. Which of them has at least one acute angle?
1. Check the angle sums: 50° + 60° + 70° = 180°; 90° + 50° + 40° = 180°; 120° + 30° + 30° = 180°.
2. (a) All three are acute: acute-angled.
3. (b) One angle is a right angle: right-angled.
4. (c) One angle is obtuse: obtuse-angled.
5. All three triangles have at least one acute angle, so having one acute angle does not tell the kind of triangle.
Answer: (a) acute-angled (b) right-angled (c) obtuse-angled; all three have an acute angle

source_video_walkthrough.title: What kind of triangle has these three angles?
items: A classification of triangles based on their angle measures is acute-angled, right-angled and obtuse-angled triangles. We have already seen what a right-angled triangle is. It is a triangle with one right angle. Similarly, an obtuse-angled triangle has one obtuse angle. What could an acute-angled triangle be? Can we define it as a triangle with one acute angle? Why not? In an acute-angled triangle, all three angles are acute angles.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (types of triangles), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (types of triangles), Q1: Construct a triangle ABC with BC = 5 cm, AB = 6 cm, CA = 5 cm. Construct an altitude from A to BC.
1. Check: 6 < 5 + 5, 5 < 5 + 6 and 5 < 6 + 5, so the triangle exists. Two sides are equal, so it is isosceles.
2. Draw BC = 5 cm. Draw an arc of radius 6 cm from B and an arc of radius 5 cm from C. They cross at A.
3. Slide the set square along BC until its upright edge touches A, and draw the perpendicular AD to BC.
4. Measure AD with the ruler: the altitude is about 4.8 cm.
Answer: Isosceles triangle ABC; the altitude from A to BC measures about 4.8 cm

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (types of triangles), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (types of triangles), Q2: Construct a triangle TRY with RY = 4 cm, TR = 7 cm, ∠R = 140°. Construct an altitude from T to RY.
1. Draw RY = 4 cm. At R make an angle of 140° and mark T at 7 cm along the arm. Join TY.
2. The angle at R is obtuse, so the altitude from T falls outside the triangle.
3. Extend YR beyond R. Slide the set square along it until its upright edge touches T, and draw the perpendicular TD to the extended line.
4. The angle TRD outside the triangle is 180° − 140° = 40°. Measure TD with the ruler: it is about 4.5 cm.
Answer: The altitude from T meets YR extended beyond R; its length is about 4.5 cm

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (types of triangles), Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out (types of triangles), Q3: Construct a right-angled triangle ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements? Hint: the other measurements can take any values. Take AC as the base. What values can ∠A and ∠C take so that the other angle is 90°?
1. Draw AC = 5 cm. The angle at B is 90°, so ∠A + ∠C = 90°.
2. Choose ∠A = 30°, then ∠C = 60°, and the arms cross at B. Choose ∠A = 45°, then ∠C = 45°. Choose ∠A = 70°, then ∠C = 20°. Each choice gives a different triangle.
3. ∠A can be any value strictly between 0° and 90°, and ∠C is then 90° − ∠A.
4. There are infinitely many values to choose from, so there are infinitely many different triangles.
Answer: Infinitely many: ∠A can be any value strictly between 0° and 90° with ∠C = 90° − ∠A

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (types of triangles), Q4

content.text:
Figure it Out (types of triangles), Q4: Through construction, explore if it is possible to construct an equilateral triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled. Also construct an isosceles triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled.
1. Every equilateral triangle has three equal angles, so each is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. No angle is 90° or more.
2. So an equilateral triangle can be neither right-angled nor obtuse-angled.
3. Isosceles right-angled: take a right angle with two equal sides, for example 4 cm and 4 cm. The other two angles are equal and add up to 90°, so each is 45°.
4. Isosceles obtuse-angled: take an angle of 120° between two equal sides of 5 cm. The other two angles are equal and add up to 60°, so each is 30°.
Answer: (i) and (ii): not possible for an equilateral triangle; an isosceles triangle can be right-angled (90°, 45°, 45°) or obtuse-angled (120°, 30°, 30°)
