media.title: How many right angled triangles have this long side?
media.context: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The long side of five centimetres is fixed as the base. Since the other two angles must add up to ninety degrees, many choices for one angle give many different triangles. The video tries three choices and then counts.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: with the long side fixed and the right angle at the top, every choice of one base angle gives a different triangle. Watch for students who think the triangle is fixed once the long side is given.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How many right angled triangles have this long side?
source_video_walkthrough.placement: after the concept's text, opened only after the student tries the question
items: Construct a right-angled triangle ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements? [Hint: Note that the other measurements can take any values. Take AC as the base. What values can ∠A and ∠C take so that the other angle is 90°?]
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child can name a right angled triangle and use the angle sum, and now sees that one side and one right angle do not fix the triangle.

interaction_points.prompt: How many different triangles can we make with these measurements?
interaction_points.answer: Infinitely many: ∠A can be any value strictly between 0° and 90° with ∠C = 90° - ∠A
covers: Construct a right-angled triangle ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements? [Hint: Note that the other measurements can take any values. Take AC as the base. What values can ∠A and ∠C take so that the other angle is 90°?]

source: Construct a right-angled triangle ABC with ∠B = 90° and AC = 5 cm. How many different triangles exist with these measurements? [Hint: Note that the other measurements can take any values. Take AC as the base. What values can ∠A and ∠C take so that the other angle is 90°?]
video_script.why: The child can name a right angled triangle and use the angle sum, and now sees that one side and one right angle do not fix the triangle.
video_script.substitution: Fix AC = 5 cm as the base, find that the two base angles add up to 90°, and try three choices for ∠A.
video_script.anchor: a base AC of five centimetres with a right angle at B above it
video_script.payoff_line: There are infinitely many such triangles

final_answer.value: Infinitely many: ∠A can be any value strictly between 0° and 90° with ∠C = 90° - ∠A
final_answer.spoken: there are infinitely many such triangles

maths_rules: choose ∠A = 30°, then ∠C = 90° - 30° = 60°; choose ∠A = 45°, then ∠C = 45°; choose ∠A = 70°, then ∠C = 90° - 70° = 20°
each choice gives arms that cross at a different place B, so a different triangle
∠A can be any value strictly between 0° and 90°, and ∠C = 90° - ∠A, so there are infinitely many triangles
video_script.design: The base AC stays fixed on the board. Two arms leave A and C at chosen angles and cross at B; three choices are drawn one after the other, and the crossing point B moves.

media.title: Can equilateral and isosceles triangles be right or obtuse?
media.context: A Tale of Three Intersecting Lines. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: An equilateral triangle has three equal angles of sixty degrees, so it can be neither right angled nor obtuse angled. An isosceles triangle with a right angle or an obtuse angle between its equal sides is built and its other angles are found.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: equal sides bring equal angles, and the angles add up to one hundred and eighty. Watch for students who think an equilateral triangle could be stretched into a right angle.
media.instructions_for_student: Try the question in your notebook first. Then watch; when the video says think and tell, say your answer.

source_video_walkthrough.title: Can equilateral and isosceles triangles be right or obtuse?
source_video_walkthrough.placement: after the concept's text, opened only after the student tries the question
items: Through construction, explore if it is possible to construct an equilateral triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled. Also construct an isosceles triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled.
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child can name a triangle by its sides and by its angles, and now asks which pairs of names can go together.

interaction_points.prompt: Can an isosceles triangle be right angled, or obtuse angled?
interaction_points.answer: (i) and (ii): not possible for an equilateral triangle; an isosceles triangle can be right-angled (90°, 45°, 45°) or obtuse-angled (120°, 30°, 30°)
covers: Through construction, explore if it is possible to construct an equilateral triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled. Also construct an isosceles triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled.

source: Through construction, explore if it is possible to construct an equilateral triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled. Also construct an isosceles triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled.
video_script.why: The child can name a triangle by its sides and by its angles, and now asks which pairs of names can go together.
video_script.substitution: Use equal sides to get equal angles, then divide one hundred and eighty by three for the equilateral triangle, and take the large angle away from one hundred and eighty and halve what is left for the isosceles ones.
video_script.anchor: an equilateral triangle and two isosceles triangles with their angles marked
video_script.payoff_line: An equilateral triangle can be neither, but an isosceles triangle can be both

final_answer.value: (i) and (ii): not possible for an equilateral triangle; an isosceles triangle can be right-angled (90°, 45°, 45°) or obtuse-angled (120°, 30°, 30°)
final_answer.spoken: an equilateral triangle can be neither, but an isosceles triangle can be both

maths_rules: equal sides give equal angles (a paper fold puts the matching angles on each other)
equilateral: three equal angles, each 180° ÷ 3 = 60°, which is less than 90°, so it is never right-angled or obtuse-angled
isosceles right-angled: 90° between two equal sides of 4 cm; the other two angles are equal and add up to 180° - 90° = 90°, so each is 90° ÷ 2 = 45°
isosceles obtuse-angled: 120° between two equal sides of 5 cm; the other two angles are equal and add up to 180° - 120° = 60°, so each is 60° ÷ 2 = 30°
video_script.design: An equilateral triangle and two isosceles triangles are drawn in the anchor band. A paper fold shows the matching angles, and the working finds the angles in turn.

marks.take: 180° - 120° = 60° is written for the other two angles

<bookmark mark='take'/>The other two angles are equal. They add up to one hundred and eighty take away one hundred and twenty, which is sixty.

beats.on_screen: Answer: equilateral: neither;  isosceles right-angled: 90° ÷ 2 = 45°, so 90°, 45°, 45°;  isosceles obtuse-angled: 60° ÷ 2 = 30°, so 120°, 30°, 30°

marks.right: 90° ÷ 2 = 45° is written and the angles 90°, 45°, 45° are marked
marks.obtuse: 60° ÷ 2 = 30° is written and the angles 120°, 30°, 30° are marked

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>An equilateral triangle can be neither, but an isosceles triangle can be both.
<bookmark mark='right'/>Half of ninety is forty five, so the right angled one has ninety, forty five and forty five.
<bookmark mark='obtuse'/>Half of sixty is thirty, so the obtuse angled one has one hundred and twenty, thirty and thirty.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Check, both sets of angles add up to one hundred and eighty.

content.text:
Shortest Path in a Box!
There is a spider in a corner of a box. It wants to reach the farthest opposite corner (marked in the figure). Since it cannot fly, it can reach the opposite point only by walking on the surfaces of the box. What is the shortest path it can take?
Take a cardboard box and mark the path that you think is the shortest from one corner to its opposite corner. Compare the length of this path with that of the paths made by your friends.

content.text:
1. Predict first: is the shortest path along the edges, or straight across a face?
2. Take a box 6 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. The spider crosses two faces, so lay those two faces flat side by side. The path is then a straight line on a flat picture.
3. Three pairs of faces are possible, and the answer is the shortest of the three straight lines.

content.text:
Worked example: A spider walks from one corner of a box 6 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high to the opposite corner, over two faces. Which path is shortest?
1. Lay two faces flat side by side. The path is a straight line across the joined faces.
2. Case 1: the line goes 6 cm along and 4 + 3 = 7 cm across. Draw this rectangle and measure the diagonal: about 9.2 cm.
3. Case 2: 4 cm along and 6 + 3 = 9 cm across. The diagonal measures about 9.8 cm.
4. Case 3: 3 cm along and 6 + 4 = 10 cm across. The diagonal measures about 10.4 cm.
5. The shortest is the first, about 9.2 cm. It is shorter than going along the edges, which is 6 + 4 + 3 = 13 cm.
Answer: About 9.2 cm, across the 6 by 4 face and the 6 by 3 face laid flat

concepts.concept_name: What the chapter found

content.text:
Use of a compass simplifies the construction of triangles when the sidelengths are given.
A set of three lengths where the length of each is smaller than the sum of the other two is said to satisfy the triangle inequality.
Sidelengths of a triangle satisfy triangle inequality, and, if a given set of lengths satisfy the triangle inequality, a triangle can be constructed with those sidelengths.
Triangles can be constructed when the following measurements are given: (a) two of the sides and their included angle (b) two angles and the included side
The sum of the angles of a triangle is always 180°.
An altitude of a triangle is a perpendicular line segment from a vertex to its opposite side.
Equilateral triangles have sides of equal length. Isosceles triangles have two sides of equal length. Scalene triangles have sides of three different lengths.
Triangles are classified based on their angle measures as acute-angled, right-angled and obtuse-angled triangles.

content.text:
1. A compass makes it easy to build a triangle from three lengths.
2. Three lengths make a triangle when each is less than the sum of the other two.
3. A triangle can be built from two sides and the angle between them, or from two angles and the side between them.
4. The three angles of a triangle always add up to 180°.
5. An altitude is the perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side.
6. By sides: equilateral, isosceles, scalene. By angles: acute-angled, right-angled, obtuse-angled.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students recall the main findings of the chapter in one place, including the triangle inequality, the angle sum, the exterior angle and altitudes.

objectives.objective_text: Students describe the ruler-only method for a triangle with all sides 4 cm and say why it needs many trials.
Students construct an equilateral triangle with side 4 cm using two arcs of radius 4 cm and explain why C is 4 cm from both A and B.
Students construct an equilateral triangle of a chosen side length with a ruler and compass and check each side with the ruler.
Students construct a triangle with sides 4 cm, 5 cm and 6 cm and write the four steps of the construction.
Students explain why the crossing point of the two arcs is at the right distance from both ends of the base, and construct a triangle with two equal sides.
Students construct triangles from three given lengths, choose a base, set the compass to the other two lengths and name each triangle by its sides.
Students try to construct triangles with sidelengths 3, 4, 8 and 2, 3, 6, see that the arcs do not meet, and look for more sets that fail.
Students compare a straight path with a path through a third point and state that the direct path is the shortest.
Students test lengths against the three direct-versus-roundabout comparisons and conclude that a triangle cannot exist when one comparison fails.
Students decide whether three lengths can make a triangle by comparing each length with the sum of the other two, and state the definition of satisfying the triangle inequality.
Students draw two circles of radius 4 cm and 5 cm on a base of 8 cm and use the distance BX to explain why they cross in two points.
Students explain why, once the longest length is less than the sum of the other two, the other two comparisons hold without calculation.
Students decide whether three lengths can make a triangle by comparing only the longest with the sum of the other two.
Students describe how two circles on a base touch, miss each other or cross, and relate each case to the sum of the radii and the length of the base.
Students conclude that a triangle exists exactly when the longest length is less than the sum of the other two, find sets that give touching or missing circles, and write a procedure.
Students decide whether two circles on a base touch, miss or cross for a set of lengths, give the third length that makes a triangle, and describe all such lengths.
Students pick out the angle that lies between two given sides and separate it from an angle that does not.
Students construct a triangle ABC with AB = 5 cm, AC = 4 cm and angle A = 45° and write the four steps.
Students construct triangles from two sides and the included angle and say when this cannot be done.
Students pick out the included side between two angles and construct a triangle with AB = 5 cm, angle A = 45° and angle B = 80°.
Students construct a triangle when two angles and the side between them are given, using a ruler, a protractor and a compass accurately.
Students explain why two base angles that are each 90° or more give arms that never meet.
Students use the line through B parallel to the arm at A to find that no triangle exists when the angle at B is 140° or more.
Students decide whether two angles can be the angles of a triangle, find an angle that works and one that fails for a given angle, and state the rule on the sum of the two angles.
Students compare the third angle for angles 60° and 70° with a side of 5 cm and with a side of 7 cm.
Students find angle A of a triangle with angle B = 50° and angle C = 70° using a line through A parallel to BC and alternate angles.
Students find the third angle of a triangle from the other two using the parallel line, and use it for triangles with equal angles.
Students prove the angle sum property with a line through a vertex parallel to the opposite side and verify it by folding a paper triangle.
Students find an exterior angle of a triangle and show that it equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.
Students find a missing angle with the angle sum, find an exterior angle, and check that it equals the sum of the two opposite angles.
Students define the altitude from a vertex and draw it with a ruler and a set square.
Students draw the altitude of an obtuse triangle by extending the base and explain the paper-fold altitude.
Students find that in a right-angled triangle two of the sides are themselves altitudes, and then locate the third altitude by drawing it carefully.
Students draw the three altitudes of acute, right and obtuse triangles and say where each falls.
Students sort triangles into equilateral, isosceles and scalene groups by comparing the lengths of their three sides and giving a reason for each choice.
Students sort triangles into acute-angled, right-angled and obtuse-angled and explain why an acute-angled triangle cannot be defined as one with one acute angle.
Students construct triangles with an altitude, a right-angled triangle on a given hypotenuse, and decide which kinds of triangles can be equilateral or isosceles.
Students recall the main findings of the chapter in one place, including the triangle inequality, the angle sum, the exterior angle and altitudes.
